canonical_question: Do ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) in high-entropy alloys represent a distinct structural motif separate from the mechanisms of randomly distributed interstitial atoms (RDIAs), and what evidence supports this distinction in damping behavior?

question_variants.question: What evidence supports the claim that the 'white arrows' in Fig. 1 indicate a distinct mechanism rather than just the tail of the main peak?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The document identifies the feature indicated by white arrows as a 'distinct additional damping peak at low temperature' in the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, distinguishing it from the main peaks. While it does not explicitly detail the 'tail' argument, it categorizes the feature as an additional peak attributed to ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs or ONCs).

answers.answer: The text explicitly describes the feature marked by white arrows as 'a distinct additional damping peak at low temperature'. For the N-2 HEA, it attributes this low-temperature peak to ordered nitrogen complexes (ONCs). For the O-2 HEA, it attributes the low-temperature peak at 577 K to ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs). This distinguishes it from the main high-temperature peaks attributed to randomly distributed atoms.
answers.conditions: low temperature (577 K for O-2; low T for N-2)
evidence_spans: It is also important to note that the peak temperature of damping in the current Snoek-type high-damping HEAs is approximately 100 K higher than that in traditional high-damping alloys ( [11] , [12] , [31] – [42] ).

Because of the high configuration entropy and severely distorted lattices of HEAs ( [50] ), atomic position switches of interstitials in these matrices are impeded by the high atomic-scale distortion fields ( [51] ).
This effect gives rise to the high activation temperatures and barrier energies for the interstitial reorientation steps and the resulting high-temperature damping capability.

source_evidence_spans: a distinct additional damping peak at low temperature (see white arrows in Fig. 1, B and C ) was observed

question_variants.question: Does the 'ordered interstitial complexes' mentioned for O-2 HEA refer to the same structural motif as the 'ordered nitrogen complexes' in N-2 HEA?
question_variants.resolution_summary: Both O-2 HEA and N-2 HEA form ordered interstitial complexes that manifest as additional low-temperature peaks in internal friction measurements, indicating the same structural motif of ordered interstitial complexes.

answers.answer: The base HEA contains no ordered interstitial complexes. In contrast, both O-2 HEA and N-2 HEA exhibit an additional low-temperature peak attributed specifically to the formation of ordered oxygen complexes and ordered nitrogen complexes, respectively, confirming they refer to the same structural motif of ordered interstitial complexes.
answers.material: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi doped with O or N
answers.measurement_outcome: Additional low-temperature peak observed in O-2 HEA (577 K) and N-2 HEA, absent in base HEA.
answers.mechanism: Ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) cause the additional low-temperature peak.
answers.boundary_limitation: Difficulty in determining actual cluster sizes.
evidence_spans: For the base HEA, two peaks could be resolved at 710 and 798 K, respectively (see green and magenta curves in Fig. 5A ).
As there is no ordered interstitial complex in the base HEA, the two decomposed peaks probably originate from the jumps of the randomly distributed interstitial atoms.
The height of the two Snoek damping peaks is 0.014 and 0.006, respectively.

source_evidence_spans: formation of ordered interstitial complexes that provide high strain hardening ( [22] )

question_variants.question: What specific stress-induced ordering mechanism allows randomly distributed interstitial atoms (RDIAs) to generate such high damping compared to ordered complexes?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text attributes the high damping to 'stress-induced ordering of the randomly distributed interstitial atoms (RDIAs)' but does not detail the specific microscopic mechanism allowing RDIAs to generate higher damping than ordered complexes beyond the distinction that ordered complexes lock atoms (low damping fraction) while RDIAs allow reorientation.

answers.answer: The text states that the two decomposed peaks in the base HEA originate from the jumps of randomly distributed interstitial atoms, and that stress-induced ordering of RDIAs is the cause of high damping.
answers.measurement_outcome: Peaks originate from jumps of RDIAs
answers.mechanism: stress-induced ordering of the randomly distributed interstitial atoms

answers.answer: Randomly distributed nitrogen atoms are inferred to improve mechanical damping, contrasting with ordered complexes.
answers.mechanism: Randomly distributed nitrogen atoms improve mechanical damping
evidence_spans: For the nitrogen-doped N-2 HEA, an additional low-temperature peak (blue curve) and two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves) were also observed (see Fig. 5C ).
The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.
Hence, only ~5.3% of all the nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA contribute to the formation of ordered nitrogen complexes.

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: There is strong consensus that ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) constitute a distinct structural motif compared to randomly distributed interstitial atoms (RDIAs). This distinction is evidenced by the presence of separate, low-temperature damping peaks in oxygen- and nitrogen-doped HEAs, which are absent in the base HEA containing only RDIAs. Both OOCs and ONCs generate a specific 'additional low-temperature peak,' whereas RDIAs are associated with the main high-temperature peaks.
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: The evidence is presented through a comparative analysis of three states: the base HEA, the O-2 HEA, and the N-2 HEA. One approach focuses on the visual identification of features in data (e.g., 'white arrows' indicating distinct peaks) to argue for a separate mechanism. Another approach relies on the attribution of specific temperature peaks (577 K for OOCs) to specific ordered motifs, contrasting them with the 'jumps of RDIAs' which explain the broader or higher-temperature features. A third perspective highlights the damping efficiency, noting that RDIAs improve damping via stress-induced ordering, while ordered complexes form a distinct low-temperature relaxation source.
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The distinction between mechanisms is strictly dependent on the processing state (doping). The base HEA (as_cast) exhibits damping only from RDIAs. The O-2 and N-2 HEAs (doped with 2.0 at.%) exhibit an additional low-temperature peak attributed specifically to the formation of OOCs and ONCs, respectively. The measurement conditions (1.0 Hz anelastic measurement at variable temperatures) are required to resolve these separate peaks.
cross_paper_synthesis.contradictions: There are no direct contradictions between the provided answers. The apparent nuance between RDIAs causing 'stress-induced ordering' (leading to high damping) and ordered complexes (OOCs/ONCs) representing a separate motif does not constitute a contradiction; rather, it distinguishes the *dynamic* process of stress-induced ordering in a random state from the *static* structural reality of pre-formed ordered complexes which manifest as a distinct low-temperature peak.
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: The evidence is inferred from anelastic measurement outcomes showing peak separation. The existence of the low-temperature peak in doped samples but not in the base sample is the primary evidence for the 'distinct mechanism.' The identification of the 'white arrows' as a distinct additional peak further supports the claim that these features are not merely tails of the main peak.
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: The exact cluster sizes of the ordered complexes (OOCs/ONCs) cannot be determined with certainty based on the current text. There is also uncertainty in the specific identification of clusters beyond the general categorization of OOCs and ONCs.
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: The formation of stable ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) creates a unique relaxation mechanism distinct from the stress-induced ordering of random interstitial atoms, manifesting as a resolvable low-temperature damping peak that does not overlap with the high-temperature peaks generated by RDIAs.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: Performing high-resolution microscopy or diffraction on the base HEA and doped HEAs at the specific low-temperature annealing conditions (e.g., 577 K for O-2) to directly image and confirm the cluster size and symmetry of the OOCs/ONCs, contrasting this with the diffuse scattering expected from RDIAs, to rule out the possibility that the low-temperature peak is simply a tail of the main peak obscured by the resolution limit.
